historical_timeline.summary: Baptized at St. Remigius in Bonn; born in December 1770, day not recorded.
His father retired because of alcoholism.
Hearing began to weaken, first in the left ear, with ringing in the ears.
Letter to Wegeler describing three years of failing hearing and constant tinnitus.
Second letter to Wegeler: the disease began in the left ear; mixing in society again.
Wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament to his brothers.
Ear trumpets made for him by Maelzel.
Withdrew from public performance as a pianist.
Began communicating mainly through conversation books.
First performance of the Ninth Symphony; he could not hear the applause.

claims.statement: Ludwig van Beethoven was born in December 1770 in the house at Bonngasse in Bonn. Only his baptism is recorded: he is entered in the register of the parish church of St. Remigius as the first of two children baptized on December 17, 1770. The day of his birth is not recorded; the Beethoven-Haus gives it as probably the 16th or 17th.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The synthetic date of birth uses December 16, the day before the baptism, as a placeholder; it is not a claim about the day he was born.

source_links.locator: birth house and baptismal register captions

claims.statement: In November 1792 Beethoven left Bonn for Vienna to study with Haydn; he intended to stay a year and lived there for over 33 years.
His father's acute alcoholism forced him to retire in 1789.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history of an alcohol problem, recorded without detail.

claims.statement: In a letter to his friend the physician Franz Gerhard Wegeler dated June 29, 1801, Beethoven wrote that his hearing had become weaker and weaker for the last three years; that a stomach complaint was said to be its cause; that Johann Peter Frank had treated him with tonics and his hearing with oil of almonds, and a tepid Danube bath had helped his general health but not his hearing; that his ears were "ringing and singing night and day"; that for two years he had shunned all society because he could not say to people "I am deaf"; that in the theater he had to lean close to the orchestra to understand the actors and could not hear the high notes of instruments or singers at a distance; that he heard the sounds but not the words of people speaking softly, yet could not bear shouting; and he asked Wegeler to tell no one.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic episode: progressive hearing loss with high-frequency loss, poor speech understanding, constant tinnitus, intolerance of loud sound, and social withdrawal. His own words are quoted from an English translation of the letter.

source_links.locator: dated June 29, 1801; continuous hissing; avoided people
weaker and weaker for three years; high frequencies; loud sounds unbearable

claims.statement: In the same letter he wrote, "I have often cursed my existence; Plutarch has won me back to resignation," and that he would defy his fate if he could.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports screening for depression and isolation in the modern episode; it is not used to state a diagnosis.

claims.statement: In a second letter to Wegeler, dated November 16, 1801, he wrote that the ringing in his ears was somewhat less, "especially in my left ear, in which the disease began," but that his hearing was no better; that his physician, Dr. Vering, had applied blistering bark to both his arms; and that he had begun to mix in society again after two deserted and miserable years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents that the loss began in the left ear, the basis for the synthetic asymmetry. Dated after the true-frame index date; used for the onset only.

claims.statement: At Heiligenstadt on October 6, 1802, with an addition dated October 10, he wrote the document known as the Heiligenstadt Testament to his brothers Carl and Johann. In it he wrote that he had been afflicted for six years, that he had been compelled early to isolate himself, that others beside him heard a distant flute or a shepherd singing when he heard nothing, that "but little more and I would have put an end to my life," and that "only art it was that withheld me"; he asked that after his death his physician describe his illness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Written after the episode, at 31. Recorded with care: it is the reason the modern episode screens for depression and assesses safety, and the modern record makes no claim about his real state of mind.

source_links.locator: his physician should describe his illness

claims.statement: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel made ear trumpets for him from about 1812, and from about 1818 he communicated mainly through conversation books in which others wrote; 138 of the books survive in the Berlin State Library.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode; shows the assistive listening and written communication he relied on.

claims.statement: He withdrew from public performance as a pianist in 1814; by about 1814 or 1815 he was as good as deaf in his right ear, and from about 1817 he could no longer hear music. He kept composing.
At the first performance of his Ninth Symphony on May 7, 1824, he could not hear the applause and had to be turned around to see it.
Beethoven died in Vienna on the afternoon of March 26, 1827, aged 56; some 20,000 people gathered for his funeral.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cited Beethoven-Haus page dates the death through the caption of his deathbed drawing and does not give a cause of death.

claims.statement: Cochlear otosclerosis has been the cause most often proposed by otologists, with Paget disease of bone among the alternatives; a later review notes that the middle ears examined at his autopsy showed no otosclerotic foci.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not used as a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: Some authors attribute his hearing loss and abdominal complaints to chronic lead poisoning, citing high lead levels in hair and bone, and in 2024 high lead levels were reported in two authenticated locks of his hair; others favor other causes, and the question is not settled.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the modern episode does not test for lead because he reports no exposure, and the theory is not turned into a diagnosis.

source_links.locator: infection, otosclerosis, or hair-cell loss also proposed

claims.statement: A 2023 genome study of authenticated locks of his hair found no genetic explanation for his hearing loss or gastrointestinal problems, but found a genetic predisposition to liver disease and evidence of hepatitis B infection in at least the months before his death; with his alcohol consumption, the authors offered these as plausible explanations for the severe liver disease that culminated in his death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation from ancient DNA. The modern episode screens for hepatitis B as recommended for all adults and finds no infection; no liver diagnosis is made.

claims.statement: His alcohol consumption is described by modern authors as broadly accepted, and his physicians are said to have thought he was dependent on alcohol.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the modern episode records only synthetic drinking below the risk threshold and codes no alcohol diagnosis.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 30-year-old professional musician with progressive, asymmetric bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and persistent bothersome tinnitus: a targeted history and examination with tuning forks, a comprehensive audiologic evaluation with word recognition, a search for treatable causes and an MRI for the asymmetry, hearing aids and assistive listening fitted for a musician, sound therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy for tinnitus rather than medication, hearing protection, communication access and workplace accommodation, telling cerumen impaction apart from sudden sensorineural loss, and screening for the depression and isolation that hearing loss can bring, with a structured safety assessment and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Deafness is presented as a change in how he communicates and works, not only as a loss, with Deaf community resources offered on his terms. Built on the AAO-HNS tinnitus, age-related hearing loss, sudden hearing loss, and cerumen guidelines and the CMID depression monograph.

hpi.narrative: Mr. van Beethoven returns two weeks after his first visit, on the day of his otolaryngology consultation with Dr. Albrecht and his audiologic evaluation. His hearing feels the same: he still misses soft speech and high notes at a distance, the left ear worse, and loud sounds are painful. The ringing and buzzing are constant in both ears and keep him awake until he plays quiet music. He has had no sudden change in hearing, dizziness, ear pain, discharge, or facial weakness. He has his first therapy session later this week. He has told no one at work. He read his blood results by portal and asked what they meant.

assessment_plan.assessment: The presenting hearing loss is now characterized. referral.question: Progressive hearing loss in both ears over about three years, worse on the left, with constant bilateral tinnitus and intolerance of loud sound, in a 30-year-old professional pianist and composer. Please characterize the loss, look for treatable or retrocochlear causes, and advise on hearing rehabilitation suited to a musician and on managing the tinnitus
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks, with a same-day comprehensive audiologic evaluation
referral.pertinent_history: Gradual decline in hearing for about three years, first noticed in the left ear: he misses soft speech and the high notes of instruments and voices at a distance, and must sit close to the stage at the theater. Constant ringing and buzzing in both ears day and night, worse at night. Shouting and loud music are painful. No sudden change, vertigo, ear pain, discharge, ear surgery, or facial weakness. Years of daily practice and orchestral rehearsal without hearing protection; no other noise or known lead exposure; no ototoxic medicines. A long-standing intermittent stomach complaint without alarm features. Examination today: canals and eardrums normal; Weber lateralizes to the right; Rinne positive on both sides; cranial nerves normal. PHQ-9 12 with item 9 scored 0 and GAD-7 8; adjustment disorder with depressed mood diagnosed, a safety plan made, and cognitive behavioral therapy arranged. Blood count, TSH, HbA1c, and treponemal antibody drawn today. He prefers face-to-face speech and written summaries, and asks that his hearing loss not be disclosed to anyone at work
questions: What type and degree of hearing loss does he have, and is it symmetric?
Does he need imaging or other tests for a treatable or retrocochlear cause?
Is he a candidate for hearing aids, and what devices and settings suit a professional musician?
How should his tinnitus and sensitivity to loud sound be managed?
What is the outlook, how should his hearing be monitored, and how can he protect what he has?

consultant_note.history: Mr. van Beethoven, a 30-year-old pianist and composer, is seen at the request of Dr. Vandermeer for progressive hearing loss and tinnitus. He dates the decline to about three years ago, beginning in the left ear. He cannot follow soft speech or group conversation, hears the sounds but not the words of quiet speakers, and misses high notes at a distance. Constant ringing and buzzing in both ears keeps him awake. Loud sound is painful and distorted. He has had no sudden drops, vertigo, otalgia, otorrhea, ear surgery, head injury, or facial weakness, and takes no medicines. He has rehearsed and performed for many years without hearing protection. No family history of early hearing loss is known to him. He is afraid this will end his career as a performer and has kept it secret from colleagues
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Vandermeer's intake note. Intake results: hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, HbA1c 5.2%, treponemal antibody nonreactive (index 0.12). Today's audiologic evaluation: pure-tone air and bone conduction with no air-bone gap; right ear 15, 20, 25, 40, 50, 55, and 60 dB HL and left ear 20, 30, 40, 55, 65, 70, and 75 dB HL at 250 to 8000 Hz; four-frequency averages 35 and 49 dB HL; speech reception thresholds 30 and 45 dB HL; word recognition 88% (right) and 64% (left) at comfortable levels; type A tympanograms; acoustic reflexes present at reduced sensation levels; distortion-product otoacoustic emissions absent above 1500 Hz on both sides; loudness discomfort levels reduced to 85 to 90 dB HL. Tinnitus Handicap Inventory 58

exam.finding: Pinnae and canals normal; eardrums intact and mobile on pneumatic otoscopy; no middle-ear effusion
Weber lateralizes to the right; Rinne positive on both sides
Normal
Cranial nerves normal, including facial nerve function and corneal sensation; no spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus; head impulse test normal; Romberg negative

assessment.assessment: A cochlear-pattern sensorineural loss sloping into the high frequencies, mild on the right and moderate on the left. There is no conductive component, which makes otosclerosis of the middle ear unlikely. The left ear is 15 dB worse at four adjacent frequencies, with a 24-point gap in word recognition. That asymmetry needs MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium to exclude a vestibular schwannoma or other retrocochlear lesion. Blood tests for treatable causes are normal. Many progressive losses at his age have no cause that can be found or reversed; noise has probably added to it

assessment.display: Persistent, bothersome tinnitus with reduced loudness tolerance
assessment.assessment: Present for more than six months, bothersome, and tied to the hearing loss; nonpulsatile and without neurologic signs, so it needs no separate imaging. Hearing aids, sound therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy have the best evidence. Medicines, supplements, and magnetic stimulation do not, and are not recommended. Reduced loudness tolerance is common with cochlear loss and usually eases with sound therapy and well-fitted aids

A good candidate for bilateral prescription hearing aids. A professional musician needs more than over-the-counter devices offer: real-ear verification, a music program with a wider input range and less compression, feedback control that does not distort music, and a remote microphone for teaching and meetings. Assistive listening, captioning, and speech-to-text will help where aids are not enough. Many musicians with hearing loss keep working, and some draw on vibration, visual cues, and the Deaf community as well as on hearing

recommendations: MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium
Bilateral prescription hearing aids with real-ear verification, a music program, tinnitus sound generators, and a remote microphone; audiology fine-tuning two to four weeks after fitting
Custom musicians' earplugs with flat attenuation for loud rehearsals and performances
Tinnitus education, sound enrichment at night, and cognitive behavioral therapy; no medicines or supplements for tinnitus
Repeat audiogram at six months while the loss is progressing, then yearly and with any change
Same-week evaluation for any sudden drop in hearing, because sudden sensorineural loss is treated within days; check first for a blocked canal
Communication access he chooses, including the right to ask for accommodations at work, and information on hearing loss peer groups and Deaf community resources
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Vandermeer, who saw him the same day. The findings and plan were explained to Mr. van Beethoven face to face with a written summary, and he agreed with them. At his request, nothing will be shared with his employer
consultant_note.follow_up: Otolaryngology review after the MRI result by message, and in person in one year with the yearly audiogram, or sooner for any change
